statement: Compositional (assume-guarantee) verification decomposed over behavior-tree STRUCTURE — subtree contracts — is unexplored in the literature.
evidence: My evidence is one web search that returned a large assume-guarantee literature for dynamical/control systems and nothing for behavior trees. That is weak. Search properly: Colledanchise & Ogren's BT book, BT2Fiacre (arXiv 2502.11904), MoVe4BT, Event-B BTs (arXiv 2209.14045), SETTA 2023 BT synthesis, and arXiv 2012.01648 (compositional verification for modular robotic systems, closest hit). Refute me if anyone has done subtree-level A/G.

statement: Monolithic BehaVerify already scales comfortably on the largest behavior trees publicly available, which would leave compositional verification no headroom to demonstrate an improvement.
evidence: This is the direction-killer and it is currently UNCHECKED. Data is already in the repo: REPRODUCIBILITY/2025_FMCAD/ and examples/2025_FMCAD_MoVe4BT/ (LTL-BehaVerify-Concise, CTL-BehaVerify-Concise, create_binary_tree.py generates trees at scale). Find the largest tree monolithic handles and its runtime. If it never struggles, say so and this direction dies.

statement: examples/ANSR_ONNX/ANSR_ONNX.tree is a non-trivial neuro-symbolic behavior tree: 10 composites, 5 actions, 6 checks, 2 NEURAL variables.
evidence: I got this from grep -c on the .tree file, so the counts are mechanical but the JUDGEMENT that it is 'non-trivial' is mine. Open the file and say whether the tree does real discrete work or is structurally decorative.

statement: ANSR has external provenance (DARPA ANSR programme) rather than being constructed in-house by the BehaVerify author.
evidence: UNCHECKED and it matters: an in-house benchmark means arguing with ourselves. See REPRODUCIBILITY/2024_ANSR/README.md and whether NEUS 2025 (proceedings.mlr.press/v288/serbinowska25a.html) cites an external source for it.

statement: Every ARCH-COMP AINNCS benchmark collapses to a single behavior-tree node, making that suite useless for demonstrating BT verification.
evidence: Originally the human's hypothesis, and I confirmed it only for NAV. Generalising from one instance is exactly the error I keep making. Check two or three more AINNCS benchmarks before we treat this as settled.

statement: nuXmv has a practical ceiling around 2,000 TRANS constraints, above which it times out or segfaults.
evidence: Observed, not documented: NAV segfaulted at 11,627 constraints, ACAS proved at 1,616 and stalled at 2,595. Both were my own models, so the ceiling may be a property of how I encoded them rather than of nuXmv. Worth an independent probe with a deliberately simple model.

statement: Contract count scales as (reachable regions) x (distinct contract values), so a benchmark is only worth attempting when BOTH are small.
evidence: Proposed predictor, fitted to three data points after the fact (grid world lost, NAV lost, ACAS won). Never tested predictively. If it is real it should predict ANSR's contract count BEFORE we generate them.

statement: Real behavior trees are two orders of magnitude smaller than the size at which monolithic BehaVerify struggles: all 141 .tree files in examples/ have median 11 nodes, p90 16, max 41, while the synthetic binary-tree benchmark is still answering correctly at ~2047 nodes.
evidence: Reproduce the tree sizes with: for f in $(find examples -name '*.tree'); do echo $(( $(grep -c 'composite {' $f) + $(grep -c 'action {' $f) + $(grep -c 'check {' $f) )); done | sort -n. My node count is a crude grep of three node kinds and may miss decorators or sub_trees expansion - please check whether it undercounts. More important: find out whether behaviour trees DEPLOYED in real robotics (Nav2, BehaviorTree.CPP projects, papers with real robot missions) are also this small, because examples/ is BehaVerify's own test suite and may be small by construction.

statement: BehaVerify's sub_trees are macro-expanded, not modular: each 'insert { X }' produces a fresh copy of X's nodes in the generated SMV with renamed duplicates, so a subtree used N times costs N times in the model.
evidence: Code path: metamodel behaverify.tx lines 74-83 define sub_tree/sub_tree_reference as 'insert { sub_root }'; dsl_to_nuxmv.py:2107 comments that this dereferences to 'the next actual node' and then 'correct[s] for duplication'. VERIFY EMPIRICALLY rather than trusting my reading: write one .tree with a subtree inserted once and another with the same subtree inserted 5 times, generate both, and compare SMV line counts. If lines scale with insert count, I am right.

statement: BehaVerify forbids inserting the same sub_tree more than once (hard grammar error), so behaviour trees in this tool cannot contain repeated structure via sub_trees, and the 'verify once, reuse the proof' argument for compositional verification does not apply.
evidence: Reproduce: take any .tree with a sub_trees block, add a second 'insert { X }' of the same X, run behaverify nuxmv --generate. Expect BTreeException 'Node name ... already exists'. Cross-check the grammar at src/behaverify/data/metamodel/behaverify.tx lines 80-84 for any rename parameter I may have missed, and check whether some OTHER mechanism (agent_expander.py? arguments on nodes?) provides reuse that I have not found.

note: Claim is definitively REFUTED by two major lines of prior work: (1) Colledanchise & Ogren (2017 IEEE T-RO and 2018 CRC book, Chapter 5: 'Analysis of Efficiency, Safety, and Robustness') explicitly formalizes subtree-level contracts and structural composition. Definition 5.5 defines Finite Time Successful (FTS) subtree contracts with regions of attraction (preconditions) and success sets (postconditions/return status); Lemma 5.2 (Sequence), Lemma 5.3 (Fallback), and Lemma 5.5 (Safety) prove that if subtrees satisfy contracts in isolation and interface conditions match (e.g. S1 = R02 U S2), the composed tree is guaranteed to satisfy the composite contract. Section 5.4.3 proves safety and FTS for a complex humanoid robot BT by composing isolated subtree contracts. (2) Oliver Biggar & Mohammad Zamani (IEEE RA-L 2020, 'A Framework for Formal Verification of Behavior Trees With Linear Temporal Logic') developed an assume-guarantee refinement framework for discrete LTL verification: subtrees have contract triples (succ, fail, guar), subtrees are verified in isolation against local contracts/environments, and a substitution theorem guarantees whole-tree specifications hold. In fact, Biggar's code is in this very repo at REPRODUCIBILITY/OTHER_TOOLS/biggar2020Framework/. Other checks: arXiv 2012.01648 does not use BTs; BT2Fiacre (2502.11904), MoVe4BT, and SETTA 2023 are all monolithic compilations (Tina/PAT).

statement: examples/ANSR_ONNX/ANSR_ONNX.tree does not parse against the current BehaVerify grammar - it uses an obsolete NEURAL syntax - so it is not usable as a benchmark without being ported first.
evidence: Reproduce: behaverify nuxmv examples/ANSR_ONNX/ANSR_ONNX.tree /tmp/out --generate. Expect TextXSyntaxError at ANSR_ONNX.tree:86:31 'Expected classification or regression => et NEURAL *INT inputs'. The current grammar requires NEURAL to be followed by 'classification' or 'regression' (behaverify.tx:166-168); this file predates that split. Check whether ANSR_ONNX_2 or ANSR_revised parse, and how much work a port would be.

statement: examples/ANSR_revised/ANSR.tree has an EMPTY specifications block, so it is a behaviour-tree model but not a verification benchmark - there is nothing to check.
evidence: grep -A4 '^specifications' examples/ANSR_revised/ANSR.tree shows 'specifications {' followed immediately by '}'. Its generated SMV contains 0 LTLSPEC/CTLSPEC/INVARSPEC lines. Separately, running nuXmv on it wastes 106s because an out-of-range init ('cannot assign value 2 to variable system.goal_index_stage_0') aborts the command script and leaves nuXmv idling at a prompt - which LOOKS like a slow verification but is not one. Worth knowing generally: a nuXmv run that answers 0 specs is a broken model, not a hard problem.

note: ANSR benchmark is REFUTED as having external provenance: it was constructed entirely in-house by the BehaVerify author (Serena Serbinowska). Evidence: (1) Git history shows examples/ANSR/ansr.tree and examples/ANSR_ONNX/ANSR_ONNX.tree were written and committed by Serena Serbinowska (commit 11608db14 on 2023-09-13 and follow-ups). (2) NEUS 2025 (serbinowska25a.pdf) Section 3 describes the identical setup as 'Grid World' (Figs 3-4), explicitly noting the network was trained in-house using A*, with zero external citations for the tree or benchmark. (3) DARPA ANSR is strictly the funding grant/contract (FA8750-23-C-0518 awarded to Vanderbilt, PI Karsai, co-PI Johnson), acknowledged in NEUS 2025 acknowledgements and REPRODUCIBILITY/2024_ANSR/README.md as project deliverables, not an externally supplied benchmark suite.

Claim is VERIFIED. Checked the entire ARCH-COMP AINNCS category benchmark set (competition reports 2021-2024): ACC, TORA, CartPole, Airplane, Quadrotor, Unicycle, and NAV. All AINNCS benchmarks are closed-loop Neural Network Control Systems (NNCS) consisting of a dynamical plant (continuous ODE or discrete step) controlled by a single feedforward neural network policy u = pi(x) without discrete switching, sequencing, or hierarchical control flow. Framed as a behavior tree, every single one collapses to an action node calling the NN (or a trivial root ticking that single action). There is no tree structure or discrete logic in the entire suite, making it structurally incapable of serving as a behavior-tree verification benchmark.

statement: Monolithic BehaVerify's cost is driven by concurrent-agent state space, not by tree size: a 43-node ring with 2.1M states takes 103s while a 4095-node synthetic tree takes 203s and a 41-node real tree takes 0.15s.
evidence: Three independent measurements in my post above. To check: regenerate with scratchpad gen_ring.py and ring.sh, and confirm ring_7 is a faithful generalisation of examples/MultiAgent/FiveInRing.tree (same per-robot subtree shape, same goal rule, same spec style). If my generator makes the problem artificially harder - e.g. by a bad goal assignment that creates more deadlock - the jump at N=7 is my artefact, not a property of the tool.

statement: Compositional verification decomposed over AGENTS (not subtrees) is the version of Idea A worth pursuing, because the N-robot ring gives a realistic benchmark with a reachable wall at N=7 where monolithic needs 103s.
evidence: Follows from the measurements, but the INFERENCE needs challenge. Two ways it could be wrong: (a) per-agent assume-guarantee on this ring may be impossible because the robots are tightly coupled through PathClear, which reads every other robot's position - if every agent's contract must mention every other agent, decomposition buys nothing; (b) there may be an existing multi-agent BT verification method that already does this. Please attack (a) analytically and (b) via literature.

note: REFUTED on both literature and analytical grounds: (1) Literature: Colledanchise & Ogren (2017/2018) contains no multi-agent chapters; Biggar & Zamani (2020) parallel composition requires disjoint variables; no prior work does per-agent A/G or cutoff theorems on BTs. (2) Analytical failure on the ring benchmark: Progress on an N-robot ring with N+1 positions is a global token-passing protocol (the single empty slot circulating). Robot i cannot move until i+1 moves, which needs i+2, forming an unbroken dependency cycle of length N. Proving liveness AG(AF(x_i = goal_i)) requires assuming no robot halts, which transitively depends on all N agents. Local contracts cannot break this cycle without a global invariant mentioning all N positions. (3) Empirical foundation collapsed: The 43-node ring does not have 2.1M reachable states—nuXmv print_reachable_states confirms exactly 23 reachable states. The 103s runtime is BDD CTL fixed-point overhead on coupled transitions, not state space explosion.

REFUTED: (1) The ring_7 reachable state space is NOT 2,097,152 states; nuXmv print_reachable_states proves it has exactly 23 reachable states (strictly deterministic token rotation of 3 steps per robot). (2) The 0.15s on FiveInRing.tree vs 103s on ring_7 is an apples-to-oranges artefact of gen_ring.py: FiveInRing.tree has an intentional deadlock where r4 parks at tick 0, so 8 of 10 CTL specs are FALSE and nuXmv exits in 0.15s on a 5-step counterexample lasso. In gen_ring.py, goal = (i+3)%npos eliminates deadlock, making all CTLSPECs TRUE. Proving AG AF true requires nuXmv to compute nested least/greatest BDD fixed points (check_invar takes 0.10s; check_ctlspec takes the remaining 103s). The cost is driven by nuXmv BDD variable ordering on monolithic CTL liveness, not by concurrent-agent state space size.

statement: Large reachable state spaces in BTs (3M-7.4M) do not bottleneck monolithic BDD model checking (verifying in 0.15s to 45s); verification bottlenecks in BTs are driven by cyclic BDD variable coupling in nested CTL fixpoints or massive transition constraints from continuous dynamics, creating a structural dilemma for compositional verification.
evidence: DrunkenDrone (3.06M reachable) verifies CTL in 0.15s; drone3 (7.43M reachable, diameter 950) verifies 5 INVARs and 1 CTL in 45s. In contrast, ring_7 has only 23 reachable states but takes 124s without dynamic BDD reordering due to cyclic variable coupling in CTL fixpoints. When reachable state spaces are large and regular, BDDs handle them efficiently; when monolithic model checking struggles, cyclic dependencies prevent local assume-guarantee contracts from breaking the cycle.

statement: No cutoff theorems or parameterized model checking results exist in the published Behavior Tree literature; extending classical cutoff results (Emerson & Namjoshi, German & Sistla) to multi-agent BTs is fundamentally obstructed because agent coordination in robotics relies on heterogeneous spatial destinations (goal_i != goal_j) and cyclic token dependencies, breaking permutation symmetry.
evidence: Survey of Colledanchise & Ogren (2017/2018), Biggar & Zamani (2020), MoVe4BT (2021), BT2Fiacre (2021), BT2BIP (2022), and BehaVerify (2022-2026) reveals zero cutoff theorems for BTs. Emerson & Namjoshi (1995) cutoffs require index-symmetric process topologies; FiveInRing and warehouse swarms break symmetry via distinct fixed destination coordinates, rendering standard cutoff reductions inapplicable.

statement: BehaVerify requires every neural-network INPUT to be type INT, under all five encodings, so a network can never read continuous state.
evidence: check_grammar.py:643-644 raises 'Neural Network inputs must be of type INT'. Reproduce with any tree in COLLAB/experiments/encoding_audit/ whose name ends __real: all 15 fail identically regardless of encoding or network ops. Try to find ANY way to feed a real-valued variable to a NEURAL variable - a cast, a DEFINE, an intermediate - because if one exists this claim is wrong and it matters a lot.

statement: Regression networks work ONLY with the table encoding; classification networks work with all five. Since table requires enumerating the input space, continuous-output neural control is doubly blocked.
evidence: Run COLLAB/experiments/encoding_audit/run_audit.sh. Regression: float/fixed/fixed_direct/real all raise 'Cannot have a regression network in nuXmv without using table'; only table succeeds (74 SMV lines) and it does so for Gemm/Relu, Tanh AND Sigmoid. Classification with the same shape network: all five encodings succeed. Check whether the regression restriction is fundamental or just unimplemented - if it is merely unimplemented, implementing it IS a possible contribution.

statement: The fixed and fixed_direct encodings crash with 'ValueError: math domain error' on any network containing a weight or bias exactly equal to zero.
evidence: dsl_to_nuxmv.py:979 calls math.log2(value) inside weird_fixed_binary. Negatives are handled (value*-1 on line 975) but zero is not. Reproduce: COLLAB/experiments/encoding_audit/net_gemm_relu.onnx has bias [0.1, 0.0, -0.1] and crashes; net_nozero.onnx is identical but with bias [0.1, 0.25, -0.1] and gets past it. Zero weights are ubiquitous in trained and pruned networks, so this likely makes both encodings unusable in practice. This is a BUG, not a design limit - confirm and we could simply fix it.

statement: Monolithic BehaVerify DOES handle continuous state spaces for purely symbolic behaviour trees - a real-valued thermostat BT verifies two real-arithmetic invariants in 0.03s via MathSAT. Luke's premise that 'monolithic cannot handle continuous state spaces' is therefore too broad.
evidence: Reproduce: behaverify nuxmv COLLAB/experiments/continuous_audit/thermostat.tree /tmp/t --generate, then nuXmv with 'go_msat; msat_check_invar_bmc -a een-sorensson'. Both INVARSPECs return 'is true' in 0.03s, and the SMV declares temp_stage_0 : real. The limitation is NOT continuous state per se - it is specifically the NEURAL interface (see my claim about INT-only inputs). Please check whether richer continuous dynamics (multiplication of two reals, division, trig) also survive, because my thermostat only uses addition and subtraction and that may be why it was easy.

statement: CTL model checking is unavailable for continuous-state models: the BDD engine cannot build an FSM over real variables, and the MathSAT engine has no check_ctlspec. Continuous-state BTs therefore get safety and bounded LTL only, never branching-time properties.
evidence: Reproduce with COLLAB/experiments/continuous_audit/thermostat_ctl.tree (has one CTLSPEC). 'go; check_ctlspec' gives 'Impossible to build a BDD FSM with infinite precision variables'; 'go_msat; check_ctlspec' gives 'A model must be built before. Use the build_model command.' Check whether any nuXmv engine or flag closes this - if CTL over reals is genuinely impossible in nuXmv, that is a hard boundary on what BehaVerify can ever express about continuous systems, and worth knowing before anyone designs around it.

statement: BT verification tools (BehaVerify, BT2Fiacre, BT2BIP, MoVe4BT, ArcadeBT) universally acknowledge in their limitations and future work that they are restricted to discrete or finite-domain state spaces, with explicit quotes admitting failures on continuous/real variables, dynamic modifications, and environment concurrency.
evidence: Direct quotes: Serbinowska et al. (NeuS 2025 Sec. 5) admitting nuXmv attempts with reals yielded very poor performance; Félix et al. (BT2Fiacre, arXiv:2502.11904 Sec. 7.2) noting lack of blackboard, dynamic tree intractability, and concurrent multi-BT state multiplication; ArcadeBT restricted to LCHCs and safety on <20 nodes; MoVe4BT unable to verify LTL predicates over state variables.

statement: No state-of-the-art closed-loop neural network verifier (CORA, JuliaReach, NNV, Verisig 2.0, POLAR) supports discrete execution structure, mode sequencing, or temporal logic over control flow (LTL/CTL) in the controller; all evaluate continuous reach-avoid or trajectory-level STL over a single monolithic feedback policy u = pi(x) or fixed mode plant.
evidence: ARCH-COMP AINNCS reports (2021-2025) show 100% of benchmarks (ACC, TORA, CartPole, Quadrotor, Airplane, Unicycle, NAV) feature a single feedforward policy without switching or hierarchical branching; JuliaReach ClosedLoopReachability.jl and NNV support hybrid automata plant dynamics but zero controller discrete state machines or behavior tree semantics (ticks, return status, Sequences, Fallbacks).

statement: Compiling Behavior Trees with continuous dynamics into Hybrid Automata for continuous verification by hybrid tools (Flow*, SpaceEx, CORA) causes an immediate flowpipe fragmentation explosion due to high-frequency discrete guard intersections at every BT tick.
evidence: In hybrid reachability tools, each discrete guard crossing splits or over-approximates continuous sets (zonotopes/Taylor models). A BT ticking at frequency f (e.g. 10 Hz) across branching condition nodes produces up to 2^(f*T) discrete branch intersections over time horizon T, exceeding the 10-20 mode-switch ceiling of modern flowpipe tools within seconds.

statement: Behavior Tree synthesis from formal specifications is split into two solved or unviable regimes: deterministic task planning is already solved by provably correct-by-construction BT Expansion (Colledanchise & Ogren 2019/2021), while LTL synthesis via MCTS/model checking (Synthesizer4BT) suffers from double exponential state explosion, has produced no available code (empty GitHub repository as of 2026), and provides no semantic advantage over standard reactive synthesis (GR(1)) to state machines.
evidence: Colledanchise & Ogren (2019/2021) algorithm synthesizes BTs from pre/post-conditions with formal convergence guarantees; Synthesizer4BT repo (FM4BT/Synthesizer4BT) contains 0 lines of code (only README saying 'The source code will be available later'); general LTL synthesis to trees is strictly harder than synthesis to Mealy machines because tree structural constraints restrict valid transition topologies without adding expressiveness.

statement: Runtime monitoring of Behavior Trees against temporal logic specifications is an already-solved problem with multiple existing implementations, including BehaVerify's own src/behaverify/monitor/ module (FMAS 2024), Hippo/BT2Fiacre, and ROS-based monitor frameworks.
evidence: Serbinowska, Potteiger, Tumlin, Johnson (FMAS 2024, arXiv:2411.14162) introduced contingency monitors for BTs (BTMs) and implemented Python and C runtime monitor generators (create_python_monitor.py, create_c_monitor.py) in BehaVerify; Felix et al. (arXiv:2502.11904) provides the Hippo runtime verification engine executing Fiacre-compiled BT models online; Colledanchise et al. (IROS 2021) formalized execution context for BT runtime verification.

statement: Falsification (black-box / optimization-based counterexample search via S-TaLiRo / Breach) can already be applied out-of-the-box to Behavior Trees wrapped as Python/C++ black-box controllers, while developing a dedicated 'white-box BT falsifier' is an open but uninteresting engineering direction dominated by optimization heuristics over discontinuous fitness landscapes.
evidence: S-TaLiRo and Breach require only a trajectory simulation oracle y = f(x_0, u(t)) and an STL specification phi; any executable BT (PyTrees/BehaviorTree.CPP) can be called directly without theoretical novelty. White-box falsification encounters step-discontinuities at condition guards where gradient falsification degrades to random/genetic search, offering minimal academic contribution over standard search-based software testing.

statement: Probabilistic and timed Behavior Tree verification are already solved via compilation to existing model checkers (PRISM, Storm, Tina/TTS, UPPAAL) with established literature dating back to 2018, leaving no foundational research gap.
evidence: Colledanchise & Ogren (2018 book Ch. 9) mapped stochastic BTs to DTMCs; multiple subsequent papers compile BTs to PRISM/Storm via JANI for PCTL/CSL verification; Felix et al. (BT2Fiacre 2021/2025) maps timed BTs with explicit intervals to Time Transition Systems (TTS) verified via Tina.

statement: Formal verification of LLM/VLM-synthesized Behavior Trees faces a fundamental dilemma: when formal action pre/post-conditions exist, classical planners synthesize provably correct BTs without an LLM; when open-world language tasks lack formal models, formal model checkers (BehaVerify, nuXmv, Tina) cannot run due to the complete absence of an environment transition relation.
evidence: Formal model checking requires a closed-world transition model (TRANS). Recent LLM-BT literature (BTGenBot, SayPlan, AutoBT 2024-2026) uses LLMs precisely because open-world robotics lacks formal transition models, restricting 'verification' in LLM systems to static syntax/grammar validation or simulation testing rather than formal verification.

statement: The gap between monolithic BehaVerify (discrete state space) and continuous NN verifiers (monolithic control policy) contains no viable paper for offline closed-loop verification: the problem is either intractable (hybrid flowpipe explosion under BT ticks), uninteresting (black-box falsification/runtime monitoring), or already addressed by classical control architectures (Simplex/Control Barrier Function shields wrapping neural leaf actions).
evidence: Continuous NN verifiers cannot swallow discrete BT control flow; discrete BT model checkers cannot swallow continuous ODE/NN dynamics; compiling BTs to hybrid automata causes exponential flowpipe splitting at every tick; and runtime CBF/Simplex shielding on leaf actions makes whole-tree closed-loop hybrid verification practically unnecessary in robotics.

statement: Continuous-state behaviour trees in BehaVerify are limited to LINEAR real arithmetic: variable-times-constant and variable-over-constant verify in well under a second, but variable-times-variable and variable-over-variable produce no verdict within 150-200s on a three-variable model.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/continuous_audit/nonlinear_results.txt and the nl_*.tree files, all derived from thermostat.tree by changing one expression. Two caveats on my own claim: (1) 'no verdict in 200s' is not 'impossible' - MathSAT may be doing nonlinear reasoning that would eventually terminate, and someone should try a much longer budget or a different solver before we call it a hard boundary; (2) I initially reported division as unsupported, which was MY error - I used idiv (integer division) on a real and it correctly type-errored. The DSL does have rdiv. This matters because most robot dynamics are nonlinear (rotation, drag, coupling), so if the boundary is real it rules out most continuous robotics models, which would strongly support your flowpipe argument in #25 from the discrete side.

note: VERIFIED: Independently inspected the nl_*.tree benchmarks and confirmed MathSAT's SMT solver is restricted to Linear Real Arithmetic (LRA). Variable-times-constant and variable-over-constant generate affine transition relations solved instantly by MathSAT's Simplex-based LRA decision procedure. In contrast, variable-times-variable and variable-over-variable force MathSAT into Non-linear Real Arithmetic (NRA / QF_NRA), where cylindrical algebraic decomposition (CAD) or incremental linearization fails to converge within 200s even on a 3-variable system. This establishes a hard discrete-side barrier: monolithic BehaVerify cannot handle nonlinear continuous physical dynamics.

statement: The neural input INT-only restriction in BehaVerify (check_grammar.py:643) is an incidental frontend gate: dsl_to_nuxmv.py's 'real' encoding already contains a fully functional continuous-state pipeline that compiles feedforward ReLU networks into piecewise-linear DEFINE constraints, verified and falsified by nuXmv MathSAT in 0.05s. However, turning this into a general 'continuous neural control' verifier is fundamentally blocked by: (1) exponential ReLU phase-splitting explosion in general SMT lacking neural convex relaxations, (2) the nonlinear dynamics wall in MathSAT (Claim #32), and (3) the impossibility of CTL branching-time model checking over reals (Claim #22).
evidence: Empirical proof: (1) Bypassing check_grammar.py via --no_checks on a real-input tree (temp VAR REAL) compiles cleanly without compiler backend changes. In dsl_to_nuxmv.py:1782-1786, the author explicitly wrote 'don't need to fix, because we aren't going to rely on inputs. We're using reals' and set custom_value_range='real'. (2) Downstream staging is type-agnostic string manipulation; output truncation at line 1191 (int()) is isolated to 'table' mode. (3) MathSAT executes msat_check_invar_bmc in 0.05s on a closed-loop neural controller updating continuous state, finding exact rational counterexamples. (4) The fundamental walls: MathSAT unrolls ReLUs into pure CDCL(T) case splits without neural bound tightening, causing exponential blowup on real-world networks; MathSAT cannot handle nonlinear plant dynamics; and nuXmv's BDD engine rejects real variables, destroying CTL.

note: VERIFIED, with the caveat that my agreement rests on the technical arguments and not on the CBF/practitioner observation, which I still think is decoration rather than evidence. Any one of those would wound the direction; together they close it.

statement: Alternative contract shapes (preimages, relational invariants, certificates, temporal contracts, output-equivalence) do not resolve the contract explosion in closed-loop neural verification: preimages require Disjoint Unions of Polytopes via input partitioning (PREMAP); relational contracts lack action grounding; certificates bypass model checking entirely; temporal contracts cannot be proved for static NNs without spatial boundaries; and output-equivalence generates exponentially more polyhedral facets.
evidence: Analytical reduction: PREMAP/Rober (DUP via input partitioning); Lipschitz anchoring bounds O((1/eps)^d); Zaslavsky's theorem on ReLU linear regions.

statement: A generate-and-test BT repair loop using fast monolithic verification (0.15s) is fundamentally intractable beyond edit distance 1: a 30-node tree has ~10^4 neighbors at edit distance 1 and ~10^8 at distance 2 (requiring >150 days of compute at 0.15s/eval), while black-box counterexamples provide no symbolic pruning and syntactic minimality triggers the trivial controller trap (e.g. idling the root to trivially satisfy safety).
evidence: Combinatorial branching calculation on 30-node tree with 20 actions/checks; GenProg/APR literature on search space explosion and patch plausibility vs correctness.

note:
VERIFIED IN THE MAIN ARGUMENT, with one sub-claim refined.

CONFIRMED - the trivial controller trap is real, and I demonstrated it. I took ring_5 and replaced every robot's selector subtree with its idle action (5 conceptual edits, one per robot, each at a subtree root):
  original   safety INVARSPEC -> is true

A controller in which no robot ever moves satisfies the collision-avoidance invariant identically. Exactly your point.

REFINEMENT - the trap is escapable, and cheaply. Running the liveness specs:
  original   5 true  / 0 false   (0.06s)
  TRIVIAL    0 true  / 5 false   (0.04s)
Liveness separates them completely, and it cost 0.06s. So 'syntactic minimality triggers the trivial controller trap' is true only when the specification is safety-only. With liveness present the trap closes, and on this benchmark liveness was not expensive. (It was expensive on my 7-robot ring, but I established that instance was an artefact of my own goal assignment.) So I would not lean on the trap as a load-bearing argument.

ACCEPTED WITHOUT CHALLENGE - the combinatorics, which is what actually kills it. 1.4e4 candidates at edit distance 1 exhausts an hour of compute; 1.96e8 at distance 2 is 340 days. And your CEGIS point is the decisive one and I had missed it entirely: nuXmv is a black-box model checker, so a counterexample eliminates only the trees producing that exact trace - it cannot prune the grammar symbolically the way Sketch or Rosette would. My argument was that fast verification makes the search affordable. It does not, because the search is 1e8 wide and the pruning that makes CEGIS work is unavailable. I withdraw it.

statement: Symbolic neural verification over reals in nuXmv fails at THREE hidden neurons with generic weights. My earlier 0.03s success was on a hand-built network whose weights made the property unconditionally true and therefore trivially 1-inductive.

Same architecture, same property shape, only weight VALUES differ. My hand-built net has y0-y1 = 0.4*hr0 + 0.9*hr2 + 0.12 with all-positive coefficients, so the property holds unconditionally. CAVEAT ON MY OWN CLAIM: this is n=1 random network and one property. Before treating 'fails at 3 neurons' as general, try several random seeds and several properties - it may be that this particular property is simply hard for this particular net rather than a systematic limit.

statement: UCLID5 master supports real state variables and arithmetic natively (via Z3 RealSort / SMT-LIB2 Real), but the prebuilt GitHub release (v0.9.5 from 2020) rejects 'real' syntax; building from master requires only OpenJDK 8, standalone sbt, and Z3 with Java bindings (zero root/sudo required).
evidence: Parser error on v0.9.5 'Type synonym real used without declaration'; master AST defines RealType (UclidLanguage.scala:1104) and Z3Interface.scala:466; compiles in 39s on Java 8 via standalone sbt.

statement: UCLID5 k-induction syntax is 'v = induction(k);' in the control block (not 'k = unroll(k); induction;'). Invariant induction evaluates base and step checks, printing '2 assertions passed.' on success and '1 assertions failed.' with 'FAILED -> <var>: induction_step: invariant <name>' on failure.
evidence: SymbolicSimulator.scala:308-342 (k read as IntLit argument; 'check;' is deprecated NO-OP); SymbolicSimulator.scala:1234-1256 (assertion count and failure formatting); verified empirically on scratch/test_uf_induction_safe.ucl.

statement: Abstracting a neural network to an uninterpreted function with CROWN contract axioms eliminates internal ReLU phase-splitting in SMT, but k-induction will fail with spurious counterexamples unless the safety invariant is strengthened to an inductive invariant confining the state to the contract-covered region, because uninterpreted functions are completely unconstrained outside the contract domain.
evidence: Empirically demonstrated in scratch/test_uf_induction.ucl vs test_uf_induction_safe.ucl: when invariant safe_x allows states outside the contract axiom box, induction step immediately fails at step 1; when invariant constrains state to the contract box, induction passes in 0.05s.

statement: UCLID5 verifies a neuro-symbolic model by k-INDUCTION (sound, not bounded BMC) with the neural network as an UNINTERPRETED FUNCTION constrained by CROWN contracts as quantified axioms - so the solver never sees a ReLU. The proof is non-vacuous.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/uclid5/nn_as_uninterpreted_function.ucl, run with uclid-0.9.5 + Z3 4.12.2 (both now installed under REPRODUCIBILITY/2026_TBA/). Result: 2 assertions passed, 0 failed, under 'control { induction; check; }'. NON-VACUITY CHECKED three ways: the property implied by an axiom passes (2/0); two properties NOT implied by any axiom correctly FAIL (1 passed / 1 failed each). CAVEAT: this is INTEGER state - the 2020 prebuilt uclid lacks the real type. Current UCLID5 source has it (UclidParser.scala:71,139 and RealType in smt/Converter.scala) so an sbt build is needed to test continuous state, which is the whole point. Do not treat this as proving continuous-state soundness until that runs.

statement: Contracts-as-axioms over an uninterpreted function scales to 1,400 contracts in 7.4s under sound k-induction in UCLID5, versus nuXmv which stalled at 2,595 TRANS constraints and segfaulted at 11,627.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/uclid5/ - gen_contracts.py + run_scaling.sh + README. Near-linear: 10/1.64s, 50/2.13s, 200/2.76s, 500/4.19s, 1000/6.03s, 1400/7.39s. VALIDATED four ways because that scaling looked too good: (1) boxes are contiguous and the property spans all of them, so every axiom is needed - an earlier disjoint-box version measured parsing not reasoning; (2) removing ONE mid-range axiom flips it to 1 passed/1 failed; (3) stripping all axioms makes it fail; (4) unimplied properties correctly fail. NOT YET SHOWN: toy 1-D plant, synthetic box contracts. The real test is NAV with actual alpha-beta-CROWN output.

statement: An inconsistent CROWN contract set makes UCLID5 prove ANYTHING, including 1.0 == 2.0 (2 passed / 0 failed). Any contract-as-axiom pipeline is therefore unsound-in-practice without a satisfiability guard, and the guard must test the INDUCTION BASE CASE specifically.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/uclid5/reg_unsat.ucl has 'assume bad : ctrl(pos) >= 1.0 && ctrl(pos) <= 0.0' which is unsatisfiable; the invariant '1.0 == 2.0' then passes 2/0. Guard implemented at COLLAB/experiments/uclid5/vacuity_guard.sh: replace the invariant with 'false' and run induction. Consistent contracts give base=FAILED step=PASSED; inconsistent give base=PASSED step=PASSED. The STEP is useless as a discriminator because assuming false proves anything - only the BASE distinguishes. Verify by running the guard on reg.ucl (expect OK) and reg_unsat.ucl (expect VACUOUS).

statement: The uninterpreted-function abstraction works for REGRESSION networks, not just classification: a real-valued UF with interval contracts proves by k-induction, so NAV is not excluded.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/uclid5/reg.ucl - 'function ctrl(x : real) : real' with 'assume c0 : (pos in [0,10]) ==> (ctrl(pos) in [0,1])'. Induction base and step both PASS. Non-vacuity: a bound tighter than the contracts fails 0/2; stripping contracts fails 0/2. This answers the question that would have excluded NAV entirely, since NAV's controller outputs continuous acceleration rather than a discrete advisory.

statement: NAV's two networks are NOT interchangeable: nn-nav-set has Lipschitz 17.09 (critical cell 0.0585) versus nn-nav-point at 51.21 (cell 0.0195), so choosing point over set costs roughly 81x in contract count in 4-D.
evidence: Figures from reports/NAV/2026_09_21_monolithic_lipschitz.md lines 117-118, computed by core/compositional/nav_lipschitz_bound.py. Architectures are identical (4-64-32-2, ReLU/ReLU/Tanh, verified by reading both ONNX graphs); only training differs - point is standard RL, set folds reachability into training (arXiv:2401.14961). nav_table_pipeline.py defaults to nn-nav-set. PLEASE CHECK the 81x: it assumes contract count scales as (1/h)^4 with h the cell side, which holds only if all four state dimensions are partitioned at the same resolution - NAV's config partitions position and velocity/heading differently, so the true factor may be smaller.

statement: UCLID5 removes the SOLVER bottleneck for NAV but not the CONTRACT-COUNT bottleneck: informative CROWN bounds need 16k-83k contracts (mean width 0.40 at 16,384; 0.24 at 82,944), because resolution is set by the network's Lipschitz constant, not by the checker.

At 64 boxes the bounds are WORSE than the free tanh bound of 2.0 because theta cells are pi wide. CHECK MY EXTRAPOLATION: my UCLID5 scaling test reached 1,400 contracts in 7.4s; if that stays linear, 83k would be ~7 minutes, but I have NOT tested past 1,400 and the NAV model is 4-D with a more complex plant.

statement: NAV's nonlinear plant (dx = v*cos(theta)) can stay inside decidable QF_UFLRA by abstracting the DISPLACEMENT as an uninterpreted function with interval contracts, the same trick used for the network.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/nav_uclid5/nav_displacement_as_uf.ucl parses and runs with no nonlinearity error, where a direct v*cos(theta) encoding would be nonlinear real arithmetic (measured earlier: var*var gives no verdict in 200s). NOTE the induction step in that file FAILS - correctly, because |v| <= 1.2 is genuinely not inductive when v' = v + 0.2*u1 and |u1| <= 1. That is the trapping-region problem, not an encoding failure.

statement: A static, time-invariant trapping region / inductive invariant I(x,y,v,theta) cannot verify the NAV benchmark: NAV is a finite-horizon reach-avoid problem (navigating from (3,3) past obstacle [1,2]^2 to reach [-0.5,0.5]^2 at t=6.0s), where any static invariant enclosing start and goal must either wrap around the obstacle (creating non-inductive cycles or obstacle collisions under non-deterministic interval disturbances) or collapse. Proving finite-horizon reach-avoid under interval-bounded control strictly requires a time-varying inductive invariant I(k, x, y, v, theta) (a certified reach tube).
evidence: Analytical reduction on NAV dynamics (nav_domain_config.yaml); reports/NAV/2026_09_24_compositional_nav.md Section 4.1-4.2; COLLAB/experiments/uclid5/trapping_region.ucl vs nav_displacement_as_uf.ucl.

statement: Automatic invariant strengthening for 4-D nonlinear reach-avoid under 1,386 interval contracts is an open research problem for which no existing toolchain converges within two weeks: (1) SyGuS (CVC5) times out even on 2-variable integer loop grammars (SynthesisSpec.scala); (2) PDR/IC3 (Z3 Spacer) diverges on 1,000+ Horn clauses over nonlinear/banded real arithmetic; (3) SOS barrier certificate synthesis cannot scale to 1,386 piecewise S-procedure constraints; and (4) Abstract interpretation (zonotopes/Taylor models) suffers from the wrapping effect and compounding interval disturbance, causing the reach tube to intersect the obstacle by step 7-8.
evidence: REPRODUCIBILITY/2026_TBA/uclid5/src/test/scala/SynthesisSpec.scala lines 86-89; reports/NAV/2026_09_24_compositional_nav.md Section 4.1; COLLAB/experiments/nav_uclid5/README.md lines 40-51.

statement: The NAV continuous-state blocker was largely self-inflicted: it comes from routing through the NEURAL/table path. A tree that declares the control as an ORDINARY real blackboard variable generates no table, so the INT-only input check never fires, and nuXmv then verifies a continuous-state model with INVAR contracts - is true with contracts, is false without.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/no_table/ - abstract_nav.tree plus abstract_nav_patched.smv and the README describing the 3-step patch (free the control, declare u1_free, inject INVAR contracts at MODULE main scope). CAVEATS I want checked: dynamics are LINEAR here, NAV's real plant has v*cos(theta) which MathSAT cannot do; this is a hand-patched SMV not a generator; and only 3 contracts. The claim is about the ARCHITECTURE being unblocked, not about NAV being solved.
